title: Area of Rectangles and Right-angled Triangles
summary: Find the area of rectangles, see why a right-angled triangle is half a rectangle, estimate areas, and solve Checkpoint problems with compound shapes.

blocks.title: In the curriculum
items: Use what you know about the area of rectangles to **estimate** and **calculate** the area of **right-angled triangles**. (6Gg.03)

This means: find the area of a rectangle (length × width), see that a right-angled triangle is exactly **half** of a rectangle, estimate areas by rounding or by counting squares, and solve problems with these shapes, including shapes made of rectangles and triangles.

blocks.text: In this lesson you will learn what area means, how to find the area of any rectangle, and then the big idea of the page: **every right-angled triangle is half of a rectangle**. Once you understand that one picture, you never need to learn a formula by heart, because you can always work it out again.
1. Key words

items: area
المساحة — the amount of flat surface a 2D shape covers
square centimetre (cm²)
سنتيمتر مربع — the area of a square 1 cm long and 1 cm wide
square metre (m²)
متر مربع — the area of a square 1 m by 1 m (for rooms, gardens, fields)
rectangle
مستطيل — 4 straight sides, 4 right angles, opposite sides equal
right angle
زاوية قائمة — an angle of exactly 90°, shown with a small square
right-angled triangle
مثلث قائم الزاوية — a triangle with one right angle
base
القاعدة — one of the two sides that meet at the right angle
height (perpendicular height)
الارتفاع العمودي — the other side at the right angle; it is at 90° to the base
estimate
تقدير — a sensible answer that is close to the exact answer, found quickly
perimeter
المحيط — the distance all the way round a shape (NOT the same as area)

blocks.text: 2. Area is counted in squares

Area tells us **how many unit squares** cover a shape. If each square is 1 cm long and 1 cm wide, each square has an area of **1 cm²** (say "one square centimetre"). The small ² shows that we are measuring in squares, not in lines.

blocks.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 320 210" width="320" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="14"><polygon points="40,34 260,34 260,166 40,166" fill="#eaf1fb" stroke="#0f1b33" stroke-width="2" stroke-linejoin="round"/><path d="M40 34v132M84 34v132M128 34v132M172 34v132M216 34v132M260 34v132M40 34h220M40 78h220M40 122h220M40 166h220" stroke="#8fa5c7" stroke-width="1" fill="none"/><polygon points="40,34 260,34 260,166 40,166" fill="none" stroke="#0f1b33" stroke-width="2" stroke-linejoin="round"/><text x="62" y="61" text-anchor="middle" font-size="13">1 cm²</text><text x="150" y="24" text-anchor="middle">5 cm</text><text x="270" y="105">3 cm</text><text x="150" y="190" text-anchor="middle" font-size="13">3 rows of 5 squares = 15 squares</text></svg>
blocks.caption: A rectangle 5 cm long and 3 cm wide is covered by 15 squares, so its area is 15 cm².

blocks.text: We do not need to count every square. There are 3 rows and each row has 5 squares, so we multiply: 3 × 5 = 15. That is why:

blocks.title: Area of a rectangle
blocks.text: **Area of a rectangle = length × width** (some books say base × height). The answer is in square units: cm², m² or mm². Always multiply two lengths in the **same unit**.

**Area or perimeter?** Perimeter is the distance around the edge (add the sides). For the 5 cm by 3 cm rectangle, the perimeter is 5 + 3 + 5 + 3 = 16 cm, but the area is 15 cm². Different questions, different units: perimeter in cm, area in cm².
3. A right-angled triangle is half a rectangle
Draw a rectangle and cut it from one corner to the opposite corner (along a **diagonal**). You get **two identical right-angled triangles**. Each one has exactly half the area of the rectangle.

blocks.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 400 210" width="400" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="14"><polygon points="50,30 50,174 266,174" fill="#e3f4e5" stroke="#0f1b33" stroke-width="2" stroke-linejoin="round"/><polygon points="50,30 266,30 266,174" fill="#fff4d6" stroke="#0f1b33" stroke-width="2" stroke-linejoin="round"/><polyline points="50,162 62,162 62,174" fill="none" stroke="#0f1b33" stroke-width="1.5"/><polyline points="254,30 254,42 266,42" fill="none" stroke="#0f1b33" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="122" y="131" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="bold">12 cm²</text><text x="194" y="83" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="bold">12 cm²</text><text x="158" y="196" text-anchor="middle">6 cm</text><text x="42" y="107" text-anchor="end">4 cm</text><text x="280" y="96" font-size="13">rectangle:</text><text x="280" y="114" font-size="13">6 × 4 = 24 cm²</text><text x="280" y="138" font-size="13">each triangle:</text><text x="280" y="156" font-size="13">24 ÷ 2 = 12 cm²</text></svg>
blocks.caption: The 6 cm by 4 cm rectangle has area 24 cm². The diagonal cuts it into two equal right-angled triangles of 12 cm² each.

blocks.title: Area of a right-angled triangle
blocks.text: **Area = base × height ÷ 2**. In words: make the rectangle that the triangle is half of, find its area, then halve it. The base and the height are the **two sides that meet at the right angle**.

Look for the small square that marks the right angle. The two sides that touch that square are the base and the height. The third side is the **longest side**. It is opposite the right angle and it is slanted. We do **not** use it to find the area. It does not matter which way round the triangle is drawn: turn the page in your head until the right angle is at the bottom.

blocks.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 560 235" width="560" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="14"><polygon points="70,170 70,50 200,170" fill="#eaf1fb" stroke="#0f1b33" stroke-width="2" stroke-linejoin="round"/><line x1="70" y1="50" x2="200" y2="170" stroke="#c0392b" stroke-width="3"/><polyline points="70,158 82,158 82,170" fill="none" stroke="#0f1b33" stroke-width="1.5"/><polygon points="330,50 220,50 330,160" fill="#eaf1fb" stroke="#0f1b33" stroke-width="2" stroke-linejoin="round"/><line x1="220" y1="50" x2="330" y2="160" stroke="#c0392b" stroke-width="3"/><polyline points="318,50 318,62 330,62" fill="none" stroke="#0f1b33" stroke-width="1.5"/><polygon points="440,50 440,170 545,50" fill="#eaf1fb" stroke="#0f1b33" stroke-width="2" stroke-linejoin="round"/><line x1="440" y1="170" x2="545" y2="50" stroke="#c0392b" stroke-width="3"/><polyline points="440,62 452,62 452,50" fill="none" stroke="#0f1b33" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="62" y="115" text-anchor="end">height</text><text x="135" y="192" text-anchor="middle">base</text><text x="275" y="40" text-anchor="middle">base</text><text x="338" y="110">height</text><text x="432" y="115" text-anchor="end">height</text><text x="492" y="40" text-anchor="middle">base</text><text x="280" y="222" text-anchor="middle" font-size="13" fill="#c0392b">red side = longest side (opposite the right angle): not used</text></svg>
blocks.caption: Three right-angled triangles in different positions. In each one, the base and the height are the two sides at the right angle.

items: Find the right angle (the small square).
Write down the two sides that meet there: these are the base and the height. Ignore the longest (slanted) side.
Multiply them: this is the area of the whole rectangle.
Divide by 2: this is the area of the triangle.
Write the unit with a small ²: cm², m² or mm².

blocks.text: **You can halve first if it is easier.** For a triangle with base 14 cm and height 9 cm: 14 ÷ 2 = 7, then 7 × 9 = 63 cm². This is the same as 14 × 9 = 126 and 126 ÷ 2 = 63 cm². Choose the order that makes the mental maths easy (this uses the laws of arithmetic).

blocks.title: الفكرة الأساسية بالعربي
blocks.text: المثلث القائم الزاوية هو نص مستطيل بالظبط. اضرب الضلعين اللي عند الزاوية القائمة (المربع الصغير) وبعدين اقسم على ٢. الضلع الطويل المايل ماندخلوش في الحساب خالص. وماتنساش تكتب الوحدة مربعة: cm².
4. Estimating area
Checkpoint questions often say **estimate**. An estimate is a quick, sensible answer. There are two good ways to estimate area.

**Method A: round the lengths.** Round each length to a number that is easy to multiply (usually the nearest whole number or nearest 10), then multiply (and halve for a triangle). Example: a rectangle 7.9 cm by 5.2 cm has area about 8 × 5 = 40 cm². A right-angled triangle with sides 19.6 cm and 10.3 cm at the right angle has area about 20 × 10 ÷ 2 = 100 cm².

**Method B: count squares on a grid.** Count the whole squares inside the shape. Then count the part squares and treat each part square as about half a square (or count only the parts that are half or more). This is useful when the shape is drawn on squared paper.

blocks.text: Use an estimate to **check** your exact answer. If you calculate 299 cm² but your estimate was 30 cm², you know something has gone wrong (perhaps a decimal point in the wrong place).
5. Shapes made of rectangles and triangles

Many shapes can be split into a rectangle and a right-angled triangle. Find each area separately, then **add** them. Sometimes it is easier to find a big rectangle and **subtract** the part that is missing.

items: Draw a dashed line to split the shape into a rectangle and a right-angled triangle.
Work out any missing lengths (opposite sides of a rectangle are equal; lengths along one side add up).
Find the area of each part.
Add the parts (or subtract a cut-out part from a whole rectangle).
Give the unit.

blocks.text: 6. Worked examples

**Worked example 1** (no calculator)
A rectangular poster is 9 cm long and 6 cm wide.
(a) Work out the area of the poster. [1]
(b) Ahmed has a piece of card 19.8 cm by 4.1 cm. Estimate its area. [1]

items: (a) Area = length × width = 9 × 6 = **54 cm²**.
(b) Round: 19.8 ≈ 20 and 4.1 ≈ 4. Estimate = 20 × 4 = **80 cm²**. (The exact area is 81.18 cm², so 80 is a good estimate.)
Common mistake: writing 54 cm (a length) instead of 54 cm² (an area).

blocks.text:
**Worked example 2**
A right-angled triangle has sides 8 cm, 6 cm and 10 cm. The right angle is between the 8 cm side and the 6 cm side. Calculate the area of the triangle. [1]

items: The sides at the right angle are 8 cm and 6 cm. The 10 cm side is the longest side, so we do not use it.
Rectangle: 8 × 6 = 48 cm². Triangle: 48 ÷ 2 = **24 cm²**.
Common mistakes: 8 × 10 ÷ 2 = 40 (used the longest side) or 8 × 6 = 48 (forgot to halve).

blocks.text:
**Worked example 3** (calculator allowed)
A right-angled triangle has base 9.8 cm and height 6.1 cm.
(a) Estimate the area. Show your working. [1]
(b) Calculate the exact area. [1]

items: Check: 29.89 is close to the estimate of 30, so the answer is sensible.

blocks.text:
**Worked example 4**
A right-angled triangle is drawn on a centimetre-square grid (the triangle in section 4). Its two sides at the right angle are 6 squares and 4 squares long.
(a) Estimate the area by counting squares. [1]
(b) Use the rectangle to find the exact area. [1]

items: (a) Whole squares: 8. Part squares: 8, each about half, so 8 ÷ 2 = 4. Estimate ≈ 8 + 4 = **12 cm²**.
(b) The triangle is half of a 6 cm by 4 cm rectangle: 6 × 4 = 24, 24 ÷ 2 = **12 cm²**.

blocks.text:
**Worked example 5** (working backwards)
A right-angled triangle has an area of 18 cm². One of the sides at the right angle is 4 cm. Find the length of the other side at the right angle. [2]

items: The triangle is half of a rectangle, so the rectangle has area 18 × 2 = 36 cm². (1 mark for 36 seen)
Common mistake: 18 ÷ 4 = 4.5 (forgot that the triangle is only half the rectangle).

blocks.text:
**Worked example 6** (compound shape)
The diagram in section 5 shows the plan of a garden. Work out its total area. [2]

items: Rectangle A: 10 × 6 = 60 m².
Triangle B: base 4 m, height 6 m: 4 × 6 ÷ 2 = 12 m².
Total: 60 + 12 = **72 m²**. (1 mark for a correct method for one part, 1 mark for 72)
Common mistake: using 14 m × 6 m = 84 m², treating the whole shape as a rectangle.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
items: Using the longest (slanted) side in the calculation. Only the two sides at the right angle are used.
Forgetting to divide by 2 for a triangle.
Dividing by 2 twice: for example, halving the base and then halving the answer again.
Writing cm instead of cm². Area is always in square units.
Mixing up area and perimeter: perimeter is adding the sides; area is the space inside.
Multiplying lengths in different units (for example 2 m × 50 cm). Change them to the same unit first.
In a compound shape, counting a part twice or using a length that belongs to the other part.

blocks.title: How Checkpoint asks this
items: "Calculate the area of the triangle." A labelled diagram, often with all three sides given: choose the two at the right angle.
"Estimate the area." Show the rounded numbers you used (for example 10 × 6 ÷ 2). An exact answer with no rounding may not get the mark.
Shapes on a centimetre-square grid: count the squares, or find the rectangle around the triangle.
"Draw a right-angled triangle with an area of 10 cm²." Choose two sides that multiply to 20 (for example 5 cm and 4 cm).
Working backwards: the area is given and you find a missing side. Double the area first.
"Tick (✓) to show whether Sara is correct. Explain how you know." Give a number reason, for example "6 × 4 ÷ 2 = 12, not 24".
Calculator questions (Paper 2) can use decimals such as 7.5 cm × 3.2 cm. On Paper 1 the numbers are easier to work out in your head or on paper.
Diagrams may say "not drawn to scale": use the numbers written, not a ruler.

blocks.title: خلي بالك
items: المساحة وحدتها مربعة (cm² أو m²) — المحيط وحدته عادية (cm أو m).
لو المساحة معطاة وعايز ضلع: اضرب المساحة في ٢ الأول، وبعدين اقسم على الضلع التاني.

blocks.text: 7. Practice

blocks.title: Practice: area of rectangles and right-angled triangles
blocks.intro: Mixed questions from easy to Checkpoint-hard. Questions 1 to 9 can be done without a calculator; you may use one for the rest. Show your working on paper, then type your answer.

questions.q: Which unit could be used to measure the area of a book cover?
questions.e: Area is measured in square units, so cm². (cm is for length, cm³ and ml are for volume and capacity.)

questions.q: Work out the area of this rectangle.

questions.q: Calculate the area of this right-angled triangle.
questions.e: Use the two sides at the right angle: 10 cm and 7 cm. 10 × 7 = 70, 70 ÷ 2 = 35 cm². The 12.2 cm side is the longest side and is not used.

questions.q: A sheet of paper is 29.7 cm long and 21.1 cm wide. Which is the best estimate of its area?
questions.e: Round: 29.7 ≈ 30 and 21.1 ≈ 20. 30 × 20 = 600 cm². (The exact area is 626.67 cm².)

questions.img: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 320 180" width="320" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="14"><path d="M20 20v140M48 20v140M76 20v140M104 20v140M132 20v140M160 20v140M188 20v140M216 20v140M244 20v140M272 20v140M300 20v140M20 20h280M20 48h280M20 76h280M20 104h280M20 132h280M20 160h280" stroke="#c9d3e3" stroke-width="1" fill="none"/><polygon points="48,132 272,132 272,48" fill="#e3f4e5" stroke="#0f1b33" stroke-width="2.5" stroke-linejoin="round"/><polyline points="260,132 260,120 272,120" fill="none" stroke="#0f1b33" stroke-width="1.5"/></svg>
questions.q: Each square on the grid has an area of 1 cm². Work out the area of the shaded right-angled triangle.
questions.e: Count the sides at the right angle: 8 squares across and 3 squares up. The rectangle around it is 8 × 3 = 24 cm², so the triangle is 24 ÷ 2 = 12 cm².

questions.q: A right-angled triangle has an area of 30 cm². One side at the right angle is 12 cm long. How long is the other side at the right angle?
questions.e: Double the area to get the rectangle: 30 × 2 = 60 cm². Then 60 ÷ 12 = 5 cm. Check: 12 × 5 ÷ 2 = 30 ✓. (1 mark for 60 seen.)

questions.q: A square has sides of 9 cm. It is cut along a diagonal into two right-angled triangles. What is the area of one triangle?
questions.e: Area of the square = 9 × 9 = 81 cm². One triangle is half: 81 ÷ 2 = 40.5 cm².

questions.img: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 300 185" width="300" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="14"><polygon points="60,150 240,150 60,75" fill="#eaf1fb" stroke="#0f1b33" stroke-width="2" stroke-linejoin="round"/><polyline points="72,150 72,138 60,138" fill="none" stroke="#0f1b33" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="150" y="172" text-anchor="middle">12 cm</text><text x="52" y="118" text-anchor="end">5 cm</text><text x="162" y="100">13 cm</text></svg>
questions.q: (a) Which two lengths do you multiply to find its area?
questions.e: The base and height are the two sides that meet at the right angle: 5 cm and 12 cm. The 13 cm side is the longest side, opposite the right angle.

questions.img: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 300 185" width="300" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="14"><polygon points="60,150 240,150 60,75" fill="#eaf1fb" stroke="#0f1b33" stroke-width="2" stroke-linejoin="round"/><polyline points="72,150 72,138 60,138" fill="none" stroke="#0f1b33" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="150" y="172" text-anchor="middle">12 cm</text><text x="52" y="118" text-anchor="end">5 cm</text><text x="162" y="100">13 cm</text></svg>
questions.q: (b) Calculate the area of the triangle.

questions.img: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 380 240" width="380" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="14"><polygon points="204,30 314,30 314,96" fill="none" stroke="#0f1b33" stroke-width="1.5" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-dasharray="5 4"/><polygon points="50,206 314,206 314,96 204,30 50,30" fill="#eaf1fb" stroke="#0f1b33" stroke-width="2" stroke-linejoin="round"/><text x="259" y="22" text-anchor="middle">5 cm</text><text x="322" y="68">3 cm</text><text x="182" y="226" text-anchor="middle">12 cm</text><text x="42" y="123" text-anchor="end">8 cm</text><text x="273" y="54" text-anchor="middle" font-size="13" font-style="italic">cut off</text></svg>
questions.q: A rectangular card is 12 cm by 8 cm. A right-angled triangle is cut off one corner, as shown. Work out the area of the card that is left. Show your working.
questions.e: Whole card: 12 × 8 = 96 cm². Triangle cut off: 5 × 3 ÷ 2 = 7.5 cm². Card left: 96 − 7.5 = 88.5 cm². (1 mark for 96 and 7.5 seen, 1 mark for 88.5.)

questions.q: The diagram shows the end wall of a shed: a rectangle with a right-angled triangle on top. Work out the total area of the wall.
questions.e: Rectangle: 6 × 4 = 24 m². Triangle: sides at the right angle are 6 m and 3 m, so 6 × 3 ÷ 2 = 9 m². Total = 24 + 9 = 33 m². (1 mark for a correct area of one part.)

questions.q: Triangle P is a right-angled triangle with base 8 cm and height 3 cm. Triangle Q is a right-angled triangle with base 6 cm and height 4 cm. Which statement is correct?
c: You cannot tell without measuring the longest sides.
questions.e: P: 8 × 3 ÷ 2 = 12 cm². Q: 6 × 4 ÷ 2 = 12 cm². Both are 12 cm², so they have the same area. The longest sides are not needed.

questions.q: Sara says: "A right-angled triangle with base 6 cm and height 4 cm has an area of 24 cm²." Is Sara correct? Explain how you know.
questions.ms: 1 mark: says Sara is not correct AND gives a reason, e.g. "24 is the area of the rectangle; the triangle is half, 12 cm²" or "6 × 4 ÷ 2 = 12". Do not accept "No" with no reason or with a wrong value.
questions.e: Sara is not correct. 6 × 4 = 24 cm² is the area of the whole rectangle. The triangle is half of it: 24 ÷ 2 = 12 cm².

questions.q: On centimetre-square paper, draw a right-angled triangle with an area of exactly 10 cm². Write the lengths of the two sides at the right angle.
questions.ms: 1 mark: a right-angled triangle whose two sides at the right angle multiply to 20, e.g. 5 cm and 4 cm, 10 cm and 2 cm, or 20 cm and 1 cm. The right angle must be clear. Accept any correct triangle on the grid.
questions.e: The triangle is half of a rectangle of area 20 cm². Any two sides at the right angle that multiply to 20 work: 5 cm and 4 cm, 10 cm and 2 cm, or 20 cm and 1 cm. Example: 5 × 4 ÷ 2 = 10 cm².

blocks.title: Remember
items: Area is the space inside a shape, measured in square units: cm², m², mm².
Area of a rectangle = length × width.
A right-angled triangle is half of a rectangle: area = base × height ÷ 2, using the two sides at the right angle.
Never use the longest (slanted) side for the area.
Estimate by rounding the lengths or counting squares, and use the estimate to check your answer.
For shapes made of parts: split, find each area, then add (or subtract a cut-out).
